The Lenape, Lenappe, Lenapi or Lenni Lenape (meaning "the people" or "true people") are a group of several bands of Native American people who share cultural and linguistic traits. They are also known as the Delaware Indians. They spoke two similar languages known as the Delaware languages: Unami and Munsee. The three subtribes of the Lenape are Munsee, Unami and Unalachtigo. They lived in different regions in Pennsylvania. The Lenape lived in the part of the Northeast Woodlands called Lenapehoking, roughly the area around and between the Delaware and lower Hudson Rivers. These areas are known today as the U.S. states of New Jersey, eastern Pennsylvania around the Delaware and Lehigh valleys. They also lived on the north shore of Delaware and much of southeastern New York, mostly the lower Hudson Valley and Upper New York Bay. Nowadays most live in Oklahoma, Wisconsin and Ontario.

The Lenca are indigenous people from Southwest Honduras and Eastern El Salvador who once spoke various dialects, but now only a few remain. They are the largest tribal group in Honduras, with a population of over 450,000.

The length of the day is how long a day is. On Earth, a sidereal day is 23 hours and 56 minutes long, and a solar day is 24 hours. There are other planets with different types of day. This uses Hours time and days on earth. The Earth is constantly losing angular velocity and rotational energy through a process called tidal acceleration, which leads to a slow lengthening of the day. Tidal acceleration is an effect of the tidal forces between an orbiting natural satellite (e.g. the Moon), and the primary planet that it orbits (e.g. Earth). This is adjusted by leap seconds. A century ago, the average day was about 1.7 milliseconds shorter than today. In the late Neoproterozoic about 620 million years ago a day had only about 21.9±0.4 hours.

Leningrad Oblast (,, ) is a federal subject of Russia. Specifically, it is an oblast. It was created on 1 August 1927. It was not until 1946 that the oblast's borders had been mostly put in their current position. The oblast was named after the city of Leningrad. In 1991, the city restored its original name, Saint Petersburg. The oblast keeps the name of Leningrad. The capital and largest city is Gatchina. The first governor of Leningrad Oblast was Vadim Gustov (in 1996–1998). The current governor, since 2012, is Aleksandr Drozdenko. The oblast has an area of 84500 sqkm and a population of 1,716,868 (2010 Census); up from 1,669,205 recorded in the 2002 Census. Leningrad Oblast is highly industrialized. The oblast is on the historic region of Ingria. It is bordered by Finland (Kymenlaakso and South Karelia) in the northwest and Estonia (Ida-Viru County) in the west. It also borders five federal subjects of Russia: the Republic of Karelia in the northeast, Vologda Oblast in the east, Novgorod Oblast in the south, Pskov Oblast in the southwest, and the federal city of Saint Petersburg in the west. Leningrad Oblast is around the Gulf of Finland and south of two great freshwater lakes. These are Lake Ladoga and Lake Onega. The oblast includes the Karelian Isthmus and some islands, including Gogland in the Gulf of Finland and Konevets in Lake Ladoga. Much of the area is in the drainage basin of the Neva. The Neva is the only outflow of Lake Ladoga. Other major rivers in Leningrad Oblast include the Svir, the Vuoksi, the Syas, the Luga, the Narva, and the Volkhov. The territory of present-day Leningrad Oblast was populated shortly after the end of the Weichselian glaciation. Several medieval trade routes crossed the area. In the 12th-15th centuries, the territory was divided between the Kingdom of Sweden and the Novgorod Republic. It was populated by many Baltic Finnic peoples such as Karelians in the northwest, Izhorians and Votians in the west, Vepsians in the east, and Ilmen Slavs in the south. The border moved back and forth across the land during the Russo-Swedish Wars of the 15th-17th centuries. Most of the present-day territory of Leningrad Oblast was taken by Sweden with the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617. During the Great Northern War (1700-1721) the territory of what is now Leningrad Oblast was conquered by Russia under Peter the Great. He founded Saint Petersburg in 1703, which later became the capital of the Russian Empire. In 1914, Saint Petersburg was renamed Petrograd. The governorate around the area was renamed the Petrograd Governorate. After the Russian Revolution, the capital was changed to Moscow. In 1919, during the Russian Civil War, the Northwestern White Army advancing from Estonia and led by Nikolai Yudenich tried to capture Petrograd and even managed to reach its southern outskirts. However, it ultimately failed and Yudenich retreated. Leningrad Oblast was created on 1 August 1927. It was created by merging the Cherepovets, Leningrad, Murmansk, Novgorod, and Pskov Governorates. The total area of the oblast was 360400 km2; more than four times larger than the modern Leningrad Oblast. Administratively, he oblast was divided into nine okrugs (Borovichi, Cherepovets, Leningrad, Lodeynoye Pole, Luga, Murmansk, Novgorod, Pskov, and Velikiye Luki), each of which was divided into districts. In 1929, Velikiye Luki Okrug was given to the newly formed Western Oblast. Leningrad was separated from Leningrad Oblast in December 1931. In 1935 five southernmost districts were made part of Kalinin Oblast. In 1936 some parts of the territory of Leningrad Suburban District of Leningrad was returned to Leningrad Oblast and divided into Vsevolozhsky District, Krasnoselsky District, Pargolovsky District and Slutsky District (renamed Pavlovsky District in 1944). Vologda Oblast was created out of Leningrad Oblast in 1937. Murmansk Oblast was split from Leningrad Oblast in 1938. On 30 November 1939, the Soviet Union waged the Winter War against Finland. With the Moscow Peace Treaty in 1940, the Soviet Union gained some territories, including the Karelian Isthmus. Their Karelian population was quickly evacuated to inner Finland and later replaced with people from other parts of the Soviet Union. A small part of the territory (the municipalities of Kanneljärvi, Koivisto and Rautu) was put into Leningrad Oblast. The rest was given to the Karelo-Finnish Soviet Socialist Republic. A lenticular cloud (Altocumulus lenticularis) is a type of cloud that generally forms at high altitudes. They are shaped like discs and remain roughly in the same position. Because of the way they are shaped, they have been offered as an explanation for some UFO sightings. Lenticular clouds are formed when the wind forces the air up a mountain ridge to where the air is cool enough for water vapor to condense.

The crystalline lens is a transparent, biconvex structure in the eye. With the cornea it helps to refract light to be focused on the retina. The lens changes shape. This changes the focal distance of the eye so that it can focus on objects at various distances. This adjustment of the lens is called accommodation. It is similar to the focusing of a photographic camera when it focuses its lenses. The lens is flatter on the inside. The lens is also called the aquula (Latin, a little stream, dim. of aqua, water) or crystalline lens. In humans, the refractive power of the lens in its natural environment is approximately 18 dioptres. This is about one-third of the eye's total power.

A lens is a clear (transparent) object (like glass, plastic or even a drop of water) that changes the way things look by bending the light that goes through it. They may make things appear larger, smaller, or upside-down. Some places lenses are used include spectacles (eyeglasses), contact lenses, cameras, projectors, microscopes, telescopes, magnifying glasses, etc. Each eye also has a lens. They work by refraction, or the bending of light. Lenses have three main shapes. Each different shape changes the image (making it bigger or smaller). The three types are: The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length: P = 1/focal length. The word "lens" comes from the Latin word for "lentil," because the earliest convex lenses in common use were shaped like the bean. The oldest written record of lenses is in the ancient Greek play by Aristophanes called "Clouds", where lenses were used with sunlight to make fire. Galileo Galilei is commonly believed to have used lenses to make the first known refracting telescope. However, he merely adapted and improved a design he learned from Dutch lensmakers such as Hans Lippershey. He was probably the first to use telescopes to make accurate astronomical observations, though.

A lenticel is porous tissue in the bark of trees. Its cells make large intercellular spaces in the periderm of the bark. They are found in the woody stems and roots of dicotyledonous flowering plants. Lenticels are also found in other woody plants, starting in the Carboniferous period. The development and increase in these primitive lenticels gave a system for aeration and gas exchange in these plants. Lenticels work as pores for the direct exchange of gases. Otherwise the bark is impermeable to gases. The name 'lenticel' comes from its lenticular (lens-like) shape. The shape of lenticels is one of the characteristics used for tree identification.

The Leo Belgicus is a map of the former Low Countries (the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Belgium and a small part of northern France). They are drawn in the shape of a lion. The Leo Belgicus that came first was drawn by the Austrian cartographer Michael Aitzinger in 1583. The Netherlands were fighting the Eighty Years' War for freedom at this time. There were three different drawings. In the most common one, the lion's head was found in the northeast part of the country and the tail in the southeast part of the country. The most famous version is the drawing of Claes Janszoon Visscher. It was made in 1609 when the Twelve Years' Truce was written. The third version was made late in the war. It was made after the freedom of the Dutch Republic was given in the Peace of Westphalia of the year 1648. It is called the Leo Hollandicus, the Holland Lion, and shows only the province of Holland.

The Leo Burnett Building is a skyscraper in Chicago, Illinois near the Chicago River. It is located on 35 West Wacker Drive at North Dearborn Street. It is a 50-story 635 foot (193 m) tall skyscraper. When built in 1989, it was the 12th tallest structure in Chicago. It was designed by Kevin Roche-John Dinkeloo and Associates and Shaw & Associates. It is a postmodern design made with granite, masonry, glass, steel and concrete. The windows are divided by stainless steel bars, which is typical of "Chicago windows."

Leo IV the Khazar (; 25 January 750 – 8 September 780) was Byzantine emperor from 775 to 780 AD. He was born to Emperor Constantine V and Empress Tzitzak in 750. He was became co-emperor in the next year, in 751. He married Irene of Athens in 769. When Constantine V died in September 775, while fighting against the Bulgars, Leo IV became senior emperor. In 778 Leo raided Abbasid Syria. They beat the Abbasid army outside of Germanikeia. Leo died on 8 September 780, of tuberculosis. His underage son Constantine VI became emperor; Leo IV's wife, Irene, was regent. Leo IV was born on 25 January 750AD. His parents were Emperor Constantine V and Constantine's first wife, Empress Tzitzak (also called Eirene). Because his mother was a Khazar, Leo was given the epithet 'the Khazar'. Leo became co-emperor in 751, while still a baby. He became emperor on 14 September 775. This was after Constantine V died while fighting against the Bulgarian Empire. Leo's half-brothers, the caesares Nikephoros and Christopher, wanted to be Emperor. They thought because Leo had tuberculosis and because his son, Constantine VI was only a baby that they could become Emperors. In 776, Leo made Constantine to caesar and made him his successor. Shortly after this, Nikephoros and Christopher were discovered planning against Leo. Many people wanted to execute them. Leo instead chose to pardon them. He did exile several other plotters to Cherson. In 776–777, Khan Telerig of Bulgaria came to Constantinople. He was baptized with Leo as a witness. He married a relative of the empress consort Irene of Athens. This show a close relationship between the Byzantine Empire and the Bulgars during Leo's time as emperor. This was helped by his father Constantine V's successful battles against them between 760 and 775, which led to peace. Leo continued with his father's resettlement plans. He moved prisoners from cities on the Arab border (Germanikeia, Melitene and Theodosioupolis) to newly-made military camps or fortresses (castra) in Thrace. Caliph al-Mahdi of the Abbasids started an invasion of the Byzantine Empire in 776. The Byzantines fought back in 778. They invaded Syria with a force made up of the armies of the multiple themes, including: the Opsikion Theme, led by Gregory; the Anatolic Theme, led by Artabasdos; the Armeniac Theme, led by Karisterotzes; the Bucellarian Theme, led by Tatzates; and the Thracesian Theme led by Michael Lachanodrakon. Lachanodrakon besieged Germanikeia for a time. He then stopped the siege (according to Theophanes the Confessor, he was paid to do so). He began to raid the surrounding countryside. He sent many Jacobite Christians to Thrace. The Abbasids attacked Lachanodrakon while he was raiding. They were beat by several Byzantine armies. The Byzantine generals who led troops during this battle were given a triumphal entry when they returned to Constantinople. In 779, Leo successfully stopped an attack by the Abbasids against Asia Minor. Leo died of a bad fever, due to his tuberculosis, on 8 September 780. Nine-year-old Constantine became the new emperor with Irene as his regent.

Leonard Boyarsky is an American game designer and visual artist. He is most well-known for being a lead designer of Fallout and Diablo III. He was worked at Interplay Entertainment and Obsidian Entertainment.

Leonardo is a male given name. Many people have this name. The name is Germanic in origin. It means "Strong as a lion." This name was ranked #87 on the US Popular Names in 2021. Leonardo Araújo, Brazilian football player (born 1969) Leonardo Augusto Vieira Moreira, Brazilian football player (born 1986) Leonardo Da Vinci, Italian Renaissance painter, scientist, mathemetician, inventor and sculptor. Leonardo Fibonacci, Italian mathemetician. Better known as Fibonacci. Also known as Leonardo Pisano and Leonardo of Pisa. Leonardo Santiago, Brazilian footballer (born 1983). Leonhard "Sepp" Seppala is most famous for his part in the 1925 serum run to Nome. He owned famous dogs dogs called Togo and Balto. He was a dog breeder. He bred dogs for sled racing. He was a dog trainer. He was also a musher. He was important in making the Siberian Husky breed popular.

A leopard (Panthera pardus) is a big cat of the genus Panthera. It lives in Africa and Asia. Leopards are known for their unique appearance. They have well-camouflaged fur, which is usually tan, and spots (called rosettes). They usually have a lighter-coloured underside. However, there can be a lot of differences within the different leopard subspecies. There are also leopards who are completely black; these are also called black panthers. Male leopards are about 30% larger than female leopards. Originally the leopard lived in all of Africa (except for the Sahara Desert) and in southern Asia. However, today many leopard subspecies, especially in Asia, are endangered. Leopards adapt to many habitats, including rainforests, steppes, mountains, savannas, and montane areas. Usually, they live in habitats where there are some trees. The leopard is a secretive big cat. Unlike lions, leopards are usually solitary and do not live in groups, though it is not uncommon for young leopards to seek out the company of other leopards. Some territorial males even establish relatively tolerant relationships with the females in their immediate vicinity. They climb trees very well, and they spend a lot of time in trees. They can carry prey up a tree and keep it safe from hyenas and lions. Trees are its main escape from attacks by lions or packs of dogs. Young leopards leave their mothers after 13 – 18 months. The most similar cat in its lifestyle is the jaguar, which lives in Central and South America. Leopards are versatile, opportunistic hunters. They hunt at different times, usually in the afternoon or late at night, and use different methods for hunting. Most references to leopards describe them as nocturnal. They are often active at night. Still, it is not uncommon to encounter a leopard moving or even hunting during the day, even in extreme temperatures. Leopards are ambush predators. They operate best when they have some cover to hide behind. Usually, they secretly move towards their prey and attack it when they are close, or hide and wait for it to come close. Leopards are unpredictable animals. The leopard's ability to surprise its prey is one of the factors that makes it such a lethal predator. Leopards are carnivores with a very wide diet. They prey on Thomson's gazelle, impala, duikers, reedbucks, steenboks, and topi calves, zebras, young warthogs, blue wildebeest, and guineafowl. They also prey on rodents, hyraxs, rats, hares, storks, and monitor lizards. Leopards can take down baboons and even jackals. They are the only natural predators of adult chimpanzees and mountain gorillas, though probably not the large male silverback gorillas. Leopards do not usually eat humans, but sometimes leopards that are hurt or sick attack and eat people when they do not have enough to eat. A leopard in India is believed to have eaten more than 125 people. There are nine subspecies of leopards recognized today, one in Africa and eight in Asia. They are: African leopard P.p pardus, which includes the Barbary leopard

Leopold III (born as Léopold Philippe Charles Albert Meinrad Hubertus Marie Miguel; 3 November 1901 25 September 1983) was King of the Belgians from 1934 until 1951. He left the throne and his son Baudouin became King. Leopold III went to the throne of Belgium on 23 February 1934 following the death of his father, King Albert I. Crown Prince Leopold fought as a private during World War I while still a teenager. He was sent by his father to Eton College in the United Kingdom, in 1915. After the war, in 1919, he went to St. Anthony Seminary in Santa Barbara, California. He married Princess Astrid of Sweden in Stockholm on 4 November 1926. On 29 August 1935, the King and Queen were driving along the winding, narrow roads near their villa at Küssnacht am Rigi, Schwyz, Switzerland on the shores of Lake Lucerne. Leopold lost control of the car which plunged into the lake, killing Queen Astrid and her unborn fourth child. Leopold married Lilian Baels on 11 September 1941 in a secret, religious ceremony. It was not valid under Belgian law. In 1944, Heinrich Himmler ordered Leopold deported to Germany. Princess Liliane followed the next day under an SS armed guard. The Nazis held the family in a fort at Hirschstein in Saxony from June 1944 to March 1945, and then at Strobl, Austria. Leopold was freed by the United States in early May 1945. Because of the controversy about his conduct during the war, Leopold III and his wife and children were unable to return to Belgium. They spent the next six years in exile at Pregny-Chambésy near Geneva, Switzerland. A regency under his brother Prince Charles had been made by the Legislature in 1944. On his return to Belgium in 1950, Leopold was met with one of the most violent strikes in the history of Belgium. The country stood on the edge of civil war. Belgian banners were replaced by Walloon flags in Liège and other municipalities of Wallonia. To avoid tearing the country apart, and to keep the monarchy, Leopold decided on 1 August 1950 to withdraw in favour of his 20-year-old son Baudouin. In retirement, he followed his passion as an amateur social anthropologist and entomologist and travelled the world. He went, for instance, to Senegal and he explored the Orinoco and the Amazon with Heinrich Harrer. Leopold died in 1983 at Woluwe-Saint-Lambert.

The leopard gecko, also known as the panther gecko or the common leopard gecko, is a medium-sized lizard. They live in the southern part of Central Asia, Afghanistan, Pakistan, northwest India, and parts of Iran. They live in dry rocky regions, dry grasslands and deserts. Leopard geckos are around 7-9 inches (17.8-22.9 cm avg female)& (20-28 avg male) long, with large heads, big eyes with oval-shaped pupils, thin toes, and, unlike other reptiles, they have eyelids. They have thick tails that narrow to a point and, like their bodies and heads, are slightly flattened from top to bottom. Most of their scales are small and rough. Spaced rows of larger, bumpy scales give them a knobby, rough look, but they are actually soft when touched. mm long when they hatch, and when they hatch they have dark bands which go around their bodies.These bands lighten as the babies grow into adults which have spots instead of bands. Leopard geckos are normally lavender or yellow in colour, but pet leopard geckos come in different "colour morphs" like albino, "Banana blizzard", "Blizzard", "Ghost", "High Yellow", "Hyper Xanthic", "Jungle", "Leucistic", "Normal" or "Wild", "Patternless", "Red-stripe", "Snow", "Tremper Albino" and many more. Like many lizards, the leopard gecko has a tail that breaks off when grabbed by a predator. The tail breaks at a crack in the vertebra, and the surrounding muscles are arranged so that they separate neatly and instantly. A muscle closes around the artery in the tail at the point of the break and stops blood loss. Normally a new tail grows back. This method helps the leopard gecko to escape when attacked. Leopard geckos also have teeth and they are born with about 100 teeth. The leopard gecko is found in dry rocky regions, dry grasslands and deserts of southern Central Asia, Afghanistan, Pakistan, northwest India, and parts of Iran. The temperatures of these areas during winter can be quite low, below 10 C, forcing the animals underground into semi-hibernation, called brumation, and they live on fat reserves. Leopard geckos are crepuscular reptiles; during the day they hide in burrows, but they are active at dawn and dusk when the temperature is favorable. Leopard Geckos are friendly, docile creatures by nature, but they sometimes bite. If held in a human hand they will only bite if they mistake a finger for food, or if the person is holding the gecko too tightly. In the wild, leopard geckos feed mainly on insects, centipedes, spiders, snails, small lizards, birds, and bird eggs. In captivity they feed on mealworms, crickets, and sometimes baby mice. Leopard geckos reach sexual maturity at the age of one to three years. Mating usually happens during the rainy season. During courtship, the male walks alongside the female, licking and lightly biting her side. He then grasps her neck in his mouth. If she accepts to mate with him, she lifts her tail allowing the male to insert one of his paired copulatory organs, called hemipenes. Female leopard geckos can store sperm in their reproductive tracts for 15 months or more. They can lay up to five clutches of one or (usually) two eggs during the five month breeding season, and may use some of the stored sperm to fertilize each clutch. The eggs hatch after around 55 days. There are five subspecies of the Leopard gecko: Afghan leopard gecko, Eublepharis macularius afghanicus

The leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) is a small wild cat of South and East Asia. Since 2002 it has been listed as least concern by IUCN. It is widely distributed, but habitat loss and hunting occurs in places. There are twelve leopard cat subspecies, which differ widely in appearance and were once thought to be separate species. The Sunda Leopard Cat is accepted as a species. The small cat is similar to the domestic cat but with longer legs. It is not closely related to the leopard but has leopard-like spots. Leopard cats are the most widely distributed Asian small cats. Their range extends from the Russian Far East, Korea, China, Indochina, the Indian subcontinent, northern Pakistan, the Philippines and the Sunda Islands of Indonesia. They prefer forested habitats, but are found in agriculturally used areas. They live in tropical evergreen rainforests and plantations at sea level, and in subtropical deciduous and conifer forests in the foothills of the Himalayas above 1000 m. The highest altitudinal record was at 4500 m in the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area. In the northeast of their range they live close to rivers, valleys and in ravine forests, but avoid areas with more than 10 cm of snowfall. They are rare in Pakistan’s dry treeless areas. In Afghanistan, they were reported in the 1970s from Jalalkot and Norgul in the Kunar Valley, and the Waygul forest of Dare Pech.

The Leopold Museum is an art museum in Vienna. It opened in 2001. It is known for its large collection of works by Egon Schiele and Gustav Klimt. Rudolf Leopold and his wife Elisabeth collected the works. The works have been transferred to a foundation, the “Leopold Museum Private Foundation” in 1994. There are about 350,000 visitors per year. This makes it the most visited building in the MuseumsQuartier.

Leptoceratops (meaning "slender horned face") was a stocky ceratopsian dinosaur that had a large skull are there was a horn on its beaked snout. It is known from five skulls and some skeletal material. Leptoceratops are during in the Upper Cretaceous, about 6865 million years ago. Fossils have been found in Alberta, Canada, and Wyoming, in North America.

The Lepospondyli are a large group of batrachomorph tetrapods from the Palaeozoic era. They are sometimes included in the Labyrinthodonts. They lived during the Carboniferous to the early Permian. There are six different groups. The Acherontiscidae, Adelospondyli, Aïstopoda, Lysorophia, Microsauria and Nectridea. The included species which looked somewhat like newts, eels, snakes and lizards. Some of them were aquatic, semi-aquatic, and terrestrial animals. None of them were big animals.

The Hispaniolan ditch frog, Antillean white-lipped frog, or Gunther's white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus albilabris) is a frog. It lives in the Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico, and the Dominican Republic. Scientists think it could also live in Peru. This frog lives in the water and on land. People have seen it in marshes, streams, farmland, and other watery places in forests and places with few trees. Scientists saw the frog many protected places. It lives on all of Puerto Rico, so it lives in all Puerto Rico's protected parks. It also lives in St. John National Park in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The male frogs call to the female frogs. The female frog makes a nest out of foam to put eggs in. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out, but it is in some danger. Climate change can change the whole Caribbean area, where the frog lives. It could change the rain and make the islands too hot, which could hurt the frog. If the sea level rises, the frogs could die from the salt water. Scientists found the dangerous fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis on frogs in some places. This can cause the disease chytridiomycosis, which kills frogs. People brought the snake Xenochrophis vittatus to the frog's home. This snake is a danger to the frog too.

The white-lipped frog, American white-lipped frog, Mexican white-lipped frog, white-lipped foamfrog, Cope's white-lipped frog, Middle American white-lipped frog, white-jawed frog, white-jawed robber frog, or white-lipped thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus fragilis) is a frog. It lives in Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Venezuela, and Texas in the United States. Human beings also brought it to Cuba and Colombia. These frogs are awake at night and live on the ground. People see them in grassy places, and in forests, near marshes, ponds, and bodies of water that dry up and on farms. This frog hides under rocks and in holes that it digs. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1530 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. The frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. The larvae stay in the middle of the foam nest until it rains. The rainwater helps them go into pools of water, where they swim and grow. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, for example Texas, human beings use chemicals that can hurt the frogs.

Vanzolini's Amazon frog, disc-shaped thin-toed frog, or rana dedilarga discada (Leptodactylus discodactylus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, and Peru. The adult male frog is 28–35 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female is 32–35 mm long. The sides of the frog's head are light brown in color. There is a triangle shape on the back. The skin of the frog's back is dark brown with some marks. The sides of the body are lighter in color, gray-brown or red-brown. The iris of the eye is bronze in color with brown lines. Scientists named this frog using the Greek words "diskos" for disks and "daktylos" for fingers. People see this frog in marshy places and in forests that flood at least some of the time. Scientists saw the frog between 100 and 1150 meters above sea level. There are many protected places where the frog lives: Parque Nacional Yasuní, Reserva Biólogica Limoncocha, Reserva de Producción Faunística Cuyabeno in Ecuador, Gueppi Reserved Zone in Peru, Reserva Extrativista do Alto Jurua, and Reserva Extrativista do Baixo Jurua. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, people change the places where the frog lives to get wood to build with, make farms, find oil, make places for animals to eat grass, or make places for people to live.

The Bolivian white-lipped frog or Bolivian thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus bolivianus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina. The adult male frog is 79.0-121.5 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female is 61.2–107.7 mm long. The skin of the frog's back is light brown in color with darker brown spots and marks on the legs. There is a light colored mark above the mouth. The belly is also lighter in color. This frog is usually awake at night. People see it in grassy places, forests, including forests that are growing back, swamps, places where animals eat grass, rice fields, and other places. The adults live in holes in the ground. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1400 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. This frog lays eggs in a nest that it makes out of bubbles. It hides this nest in plants. The tadpoles swim in ponds where the water is not deep and is full of mud. This frog eats animals without bones, for example, beetles and ants. It can also eat smaller frogs. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, people catch this frog to eat.

Vizcacheras' white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus bufonius) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina. These frogs live in many kinds of places, for example the Amazonia, Pantanal, and Cerrado places. This frog is good at living in places that people have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 800 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places: Mburucuyá, Río Pilcomayo, Defensores del Chaco, and Copo national parks and Salinas Grandes, Chancani, and Loro Hablador provincial parks. The male frogs dig holes for the eggs. They dig the holes near ponds. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, frogs might be in danger when human beings change the places where the frog lives to make farms. The chemicals from the farms can hurt the frog.

The yellow painted frog (Leptodactylus flavopictus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil. The adult frogs live on the ground in forests that were never cut down and forests that are growing back. They live near streams. This frog can live in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 800 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in some protected places: APA da Pedra Branca, Area Natural Tombada Serra do Mar e de Paranapiacaba, and PARES da Serra do Mar. The tadpoles swim in water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in fclittle danger of dying out. The frogs might be in some danger when human beings change the places where the frog lives to make towns, farms, tree farms, and places for cows to eat grass.

The marbled white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus elenae) is a frog. It lives in Bolivia, Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Peru. The adult female frog is larger than the adult male frog. The skin of the frog's back can be brown in color with no marks or it may have two rows of dark spots. There are some dark spots on the belly. There is a white line on the face over the mouth. There are some lines across the legs. This frog lives on the ground. Scientists have seen it in Amazonia, Pantanal, and Cerrado places. In the southern part of its home, it has lived in places that people have changed, but in the northern part of its home, it does not. Scientists have seen the frog between 0 and 500 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in many protected places: Parque Nacional Calilegua, Formosa Reserva Natural, Río Pilcomayo National Park, Defensores del Chaco National Park, Cerro Corá National Park, Ybycuí National Park, Ypacaraí National Park, San Rafael Managed Resource Reserve, Natural Reserve del Bosque Mbaracayú, Uruguaí Reserva de Vida Silvestre, El Bagual Private Reserve, Noel Kempff Mercado National Park, Kaa-iya del Gran Chaco, Madidi National Park, Parque Nacional Da Serra Da Bodoquena. This frog has young in places that are not water all year, for example ponds that dry up and grassy places that flood. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The Jaboticatubas frog or digger foam frog (Leptodactylus camaquara) is a frog. It lives in Brazil. This frog lives in Cerrado places and in grassy places. Scientists have seen the frog between 1200 and 1650 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. Scientists have seen the frog in some protected places, for example Parque Estadual do Rio Preto and Parque Nacional da Serra do Cipó. Scientists think it could also live in Parque Nacional Das Sempre Vivas. The male frog digs a hole in the ground more than 50 meters from a stream. The female frog lays eggs in a nest made out of bubbles. Sometimes many female frogs put their nests in the same place or next to the same rock. When the rain falls, the foam nests break apart and the tadpoles go to puddles, streams, or marshes. Some scientists think tadpoles can live and grow into frogs even if they never leave the bubble nest. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is in a little danger of dying out. Human beings change the places where the frog lives to make farms and places for animals to eat grass. This means there are more fires. Because scientists look for the frog in places that humans have not changed, they do not know if the frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed.

Sazima's white-lipped frog, rabbit burrow frog, or rabbit foam frog (Leptodactylus cunicularius) is a frog. It lives in Goiás in Brazil. This frog lives in cerrado places in the grassy places. It lives in sandy places with large rocks. Scientists have seen the frog between 745 and 1400 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in some protected places. The male frog digs a hole in the sandy ground, sometimes under a rock. The female frog lays eggs in a nest made out of bubbles. When the rain falls, the foam nest disappears into the water and the tadpoles go to puddles and streams, where they swim and grow. Scientists think that some tadpoles stay in the foam nests until they become frogs. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, human beings change the places where the frog lives to make farms and places for animals to eat grass. The animals step on the sandy ground that the frogs need. Scientists look for this frog in places that humans have not changed, so they are not sure how good it is at living in places that humans have changed.

The Madre de Dios thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus didymus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, and Peru. This frog lives on the ground. People see it in rainforests that have never been cut down and rainforests that are growing back. Sometimes people see it in towns. Scientists have seen it between 0 and 450 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in protected places: Tambopata National Reserve, Parque Ambiental Chico Mendes, Reserva Experimental Catuaba, Parque Nacional da Serra do Divisor, and Parque Zoobotânico da Universidade Federal do Acre in Brazil. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. She lays a few hundred eggs at a time. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The rana picúa (Leptodactylus colombiensis) is a frog. It lives in Colombia and Venezuela. This frog lives on the ground. It is awake at night. It lives in forests on hills and mountains. People have seen it in forests that were cut down and are growing back, forests that grow next to streams and rivers, and other forests. People have seen it on the dead leaves on the ground, in holes near water, and near the roots of water plants. Scientists have seen it between 300 and 2300 meters above sea level. Some of these frogs live in protected placess: Tinigua National Park, Páramo de Tamá National Park, Montes de Oca Forest Reserve, Guajira Forest Reserve, Las Jaguas Private Protection Area, and San Carlos Private Protection Area. Sometimes people who live near the frog catch it to use as bait when fishing. This frog eats animals with no bones. The male frog makes a nest out of bubbles and the female frog puts eggs in it. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. It can live in some places that people have changed, for example palm oil farms. In some places, the frog is in some danger from cow farms, towns, mines, and dams. The fungal disease chytridiomycosis can also hurt this frog.

The bird-voiced white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus avivoca) is a frog. It lives in Brazil. Scientists saw the frog in the Espinhaço Mountains, more than 700 meters above sea level. They saw it in Minas Gerais and Bahia in Brazil.

The rufous frog, South American white-lipped frog, fuscous foam frog, or lineated frog (Leptodactylus fuscus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Guyana, Suriname, Venezuela, French Guiana, Colombia, Trinidad and Tobago, Panama, and Bolivia. Scientists think it could also live in Peru. This frog lives in grassy places, marshes, towns, and forests that have had at least some trees cut down. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1750 meters above sea level. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog many protected places. In Brazil, about 17 percent of these frogs live in protected parks. The male frogs call to the female frogs when it rains. The frog has young in holes that it digs in the ground in wet places and near lagoons. When water floods the burrows, the larvae swim out. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

Dumeril's striped frog (Leptodactylus gracilis) is a frog. It lives in Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Brazil. Scientists think it could also live in Peru. This frog lives grasslands and forests. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 2000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog many protected places: Río Pilcomayo National Park, Calilegua National Park, Parque Nacional El Rey, Cerro Verde Área de manejo de hábitats y/o especies, Humedales del Santa Lucia Área Protegida con Recursos Manejados, Parque Universitario Sierra de San Javier, Horco Molle Reserva Universitaria, Reserva de Uso Multiple Escuela Rural Enrique Berduc, Rincón de Santa María Reserva Natural Provincial, Pampa de Achala Reserva Hidrica Provincial, El Bagual Private Reserve, APA da Escarpa Devoniana, APA do Entorno da Costeira, ESEC do Taim, FLONA de Chapeco, PARES de Vila Velha, PARES Itapeva, PARES Serra Furada, PARES Tabuleiro, PARMU das Araucarias, PARMU Morro do Ceu, PARNA da Lagoa do Peixe, PARNA dos Campos Gerais, REBIO do Ibicui Mirim, and REBIO Lami Jose Lutzenberger. Scientists think the frog could also live in Área de Proteção Ambiental Do Banhado Grande. The female frog makes a nest out of foam to put eggs in. She makes the nest in a hole in the ground. The tadpoles swim in ponds that dry up for part of the year and in grassy places that are full of water for part of the year. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The labyrinth frog, South American pepper frog, pepper frog, or pepper foam frog (Leptodactylus labyrinthicus) is a frog. It lives in Argentina, Paraguay, and Brazil. This frog lives in forests that have never been cut down, forests that are growing back, grassy places, dams, ponds, streams, towns, places where animals eat grass, next to rivers, on dead leaves on the ground, and ground with nothing on it. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places: Cerro Corá National Park, Ybycuí National Park, Natural Reserve del Bosque Mbaracayú, Parque Nacional Da Serra Da Bodoquena, Área de Proteção Ambiental Lago De Peixe/Angical,Estação Ecológica De Santa Bárbara, Floresta Nacional Contendas do Sincorá, Instituto Florestal Estação Experimental de Mogi Guaçu, Estação Ecológica De Itirapina, Parque Estadual Do Jurupará, Área de Proteção Ambiental Lagoa De Itaparica, Estação Ecológica Dos Caetetus, Área de Proteção Ambiental da Chapada dos Guimarães, Parque Estadual Do Morro Do Diabo, Estação Ecológica De Bauru, Área de Proteção Ambiental Morro Da Pedreira, Parque Estadual Das Furnas Do Bom Jesus, Área de Proteção Ambiental Carste Da Lagoa Santa, and Área de Proteção Ambiental Pouso Alto. The female frog makes a nest out of foam and puts her eggs in it. The tadpoles can live in bodies of water that human beings made. In Venezuela, people farm this frog to eat. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out because it lives in a big place and because it is good at living in places that have been changed.

The turbo white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus poecilochilus) is a frog. It lives in Venezuela, Colombia, Panama, and Costa Rica. The adult male frog is 33 to 49 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 32 to 50 mm long. The head is longer than it is wide. There is some folded skin on the back. The skin of the frog's back is brown-gray in color with spots or stripes. There is a light stripe in the middle of the back. Sometimes there is dark color on the chin. The backs of the back legs have stripes. There is a long white stripe on the higher part of the hind legs. The belly is white in color. The male frog's voice skin is black. The iris of the eye is gold in color. This frog is awake at night. It lives grassy places, swamps, other watery places, and sometimes forests and towns. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 3 and 1150 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in protected places. This frog has many young at one time. The female frog puts eggs in ponds. The tadpoles can grow as long as 40 mm. The mouth is on the bottom of the body. The body does not have the same color everywhere: There is darker color on the back and lighter color on the belly. There are spots on the tail. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The pointedbelly frog (Leptodactylus podicipinus) is a frog. It lives in Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, and Brazil. This frog lives in grassy places, sometimes near ponds or floods. It can live in Amazonia, Caatinga, Cerrado, Atlantic Forest, and Pantanal places. People see it on the dead leaves on the ground, on the ground, and in the water. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in protected places: Mburucuyá National Park, Iguazú National Park, Cerro Corá National Park, Ybycuí National Park, Luis Honorio Rolón, Iberá Reserva Natural Provincial, El Bagual Private Reserve, Isla Del Cerrito, Zanjon de Loreto Reserva Natural Urbana de Uso Multiple, Noel Kempff Mercado National Park, Kaa-iya del Gran Chaco, Otuquis National Park, Área de Proteção Ambiental da Chapada dos Guimarães, Parque Estadual Do Morro Do Diabo, APA da Escarpa Devoniana (campos Gerais), APA Ilha do Bananal/Cantao, ESEC dos Caetetus, ESEC Serra Geral do Tocantins, PARES da Mata Seca, PARES Pico do Marumbi, PARNA da Serra da Bodoquena, PARNA dos Campos Gerais, RPPN Fazenda Nhumirim, and RPPN Olavo Egydio Setubal. The female frog makes a nest out of bubbles to put her eggs in. She puts the eggs near a pond or flooded place but not in it. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The long snouted thin-toed frog or longnose frog (Leptodactylus longirostris) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Colombia, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, and Venezuela. This frog lives in forests, open places, and people's gardens. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1300 meters above sea level. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog in protected places. The frog lays its eggs on land, and the tadpoles swim in water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The Mexican river frog, rana dedilarga dorsinegra, black-backed frog, reddish-brown white-lipped frog, black jungle-frog, fringe-toed foamfrog, Sabinal frog, black-backed thin-toed frog(Leptodactylus melanonotus) is a frog. It lives in Mexico, Guatemala, Ecuador, Belize, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Panama. This frog lives in forests but it can also live in mangrove tree swamps, grassy places, places where plants are growing back after being cut down, and flooded places where animals eat grass. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1550 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in protected places: Meseta de Cacaxtla protected area, Chamela-Cuixmala Biosphere Reserve, Chamela-Cuixmala Biosphere Reserve, El Veladero National Park, Lagunas de Chacahua National Parks, Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve, Pantanos de Centla Biosphere Reserve, Calakmul Biosphere Reserve, Laguna de Términos reserve, and Balaan Kaax reserve. The frog digs a hole for its eggs. The female frog makes a nest out of bubbles to put her eggs in. If the hole becomes too dry, the female frog will dig to water to fill it with water again. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. Pollution from chemicals sprayed by airplanes might hurt this frog.

The Peru white-lipped frog or reddish-brown white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus rhodonotus) is a frog. It lives in Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, and Brazil. This frog lives in rainforests in low places and high up in the hills. Scientists saw the frog between 200 and 2050 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. The female frog makes a nest out of bubbles to put her eggs in. The tadpoles swim in water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The Pimocha white-lipped frog, rana dedilarga de labio grueso, thick-lipped thin-toed frog, or rana terrestre labiosa (Leptodactylus rhodonotus) is a frog. It lives in Peru and Ecuador. The adult male frog is 49.2–61.5 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 39.9–69.0 mm long. This frog has big eyes that stick out from the head. Scientists named the frog labrosus because that is the Latin word for "wide lip." This frog lives in dry places with low, woody plants, and in forest with at least some trees whose leaves fall off. Sometimes it lives in evergreen forests, at the edges of forests, or on farms. This frog lives on the ground. People see it on the dead leaves on the ground and other places with water in the air. This frog is awake at night. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1300 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in protected places: Machililla National Park, Manglares Churute National Park, and Mache Chindu National Park. They think it could also live in Parque Nacional Cerros de Amotape and El Angolo Game Preserve. The adult frog eats animals with no bones that live on the ground, for example ants, earthworms, slugs, and caterpillars. The female frog puts her eggs in holes near water. Later, water floods the holes and the tadpoles swim out. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The Peters' thin-toed frog or rana dedilarga de Peters (Leptodactylus petersii) is a frog. It lives in Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Guyana, French Guiana, Suriname, and Ecuador. The adult male frog is 26.6–41.1 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 31.2–51.3 mm long. The skin of the frog's back is brown-green or red-brown in color with dark marks. There is a mark in the shape of a triangle on the back. The belly is white in color. The iris of the eye is bronze or red-brown in color with two dots on the lowest part. Scientists named the frog petersi for the amphibian-studying scientist Dr. Wilhelm Carl Hartwig Peters. The adult frogs are awake at night and the youngest frogs are awake during the day. This frog lives in Amazonia places. It can also live in places where animals eat grass, forests, and people's gardens. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. The male frog's voice sounds like "weet weet weet." The female frog puts her eggs in bodies of water that dry up for part of the year. The tadpoles swim in water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out because it lives in a large place. But it is in some danger. Human beings changed the places where the frog lives. Scientists found the dangerous fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis on one of these frogs, but they don't know if the disease chytridiomycosis kills many of these frogs.

The Ceara white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus pustulatus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil. These frogs live in Amazonia, Caatinga, and Cerrado places. People see it in grassy places, forests that grow next to rivers, places where animals eat grass, ponds, towns, and rivers. It is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 400 and 1000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places: APA da Serra de Baturite, APA de Upaon-Acu/Miritiba/Alto Preguicas, APA Lago de Palmas, APA Lago de Santa Isabel, APA Serra da Ibiapaba, and RESEX Lago do Cedro. After the eggs hatch, the female frog carries the tadpoles to water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out because it lives in a large place. But it is in some danger. Human beings changed the places where the frog lives. Scientists found the dangerous fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis on one of these frogs, but they don't know if the disease chytridiomycosis kills many of these frogs.

The Argus frog, Criolla frog, butter frog, lesser foam frog, or South American spotted grass frog (Leptodactylus latrans) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina. The adult male frog is 90-120 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 80-110 mm long. The skin of the frog's back is dark gray or red-brown in color with folded skin. There are dark spots with white around the edges. These spots look like eyes. There is one spot between the eyes. The male frog has strong front legs. This frog has only a little extra skin on its feet, so it can swim well but also jump and move on land. The adult frog can make its guts longer or shorter depending on the time of year and what the frog is doing. The male frogs have longer guts during the warm part of the year when there is a lot of food for the frogs to eat. The female frogs have longer guts during the cold part of the year when it is time to make eggs inside their bodies. These frogs live in Atlantic Forest and Caatinga places. It can live in many different kinds of places. People see it in grassy places, forests, lakes, reservoirs, streams, swamps, people's gardens, and towns. It is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 900 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. Human beings sometimes eat this frog. The male frog hides in water plants and calls to the female frogs. The female frog usually lays eggs in a pond that dries up for part of the year. She lays the eggs in a nest made of bubbles that the male frog makes. The bubble nest and the eggs inside it float on top of the water. Each nest is 12-25 cm long and has thousands to eggs in it. It has a hole in the middle that is 4-8 cm long. The female frog sometimes sits in the hole in the nest so she can scare away animals that want to eat the eggs, for example birds. Sometimes the adult frogs lay eggs on dry land before the rain. Then the rain turns the land into a pond. The tadpoles leave the nest and swim in the pond. Because they hatch before the pond is there, these tadpoles are bigger and stronger than the tadpoles of frog species that lay eggs after it rains. The tadpoles swim together in schools. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed, for example gardens.

The mustache thin-toed frog, Amazonian white-lipped frog, rana dedilarga con bigote, or basin white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus mystaceus) is a frog. It lives in Venezuela, French Guiana, Guyana, Argentina, Peru, Suriname, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Brazil. Scientists think it could also live in Peru. This frog lives in many parts of the Amazon. It lives in forests that have never been cut down, forests that are growing back, grasslands inside forests, and flooded places. It lives on the ground near bodies of water that sometimes dry up. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog many protected places. The male frog digs a hole in a muddy place. The female frog makes a nest out of foam in the hole and puts her eggs in it. The tadpoles swim and grow in water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, human beings change the places where the frog lives: fire, cutting down trees to get wood and make farms, and building towns, but the frog is good at living in places that people have changed.

The oven frog (Leptodactylus latinasus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina. These frogs live in Chaco, Pampa, and Atlantic Forest places. It can live in many different kinds of places. This frog lives on the ground in grassy places near water. It is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 600 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places: Reserva Natural Formosa, Chaco National Park, Mburucuyá National Park, El Rey National Park, Parque Nacional Calilegua, Paisaje Protegido Quebrada de los Cuervos, Paisaje Protegido Valle del Lunarejo, Cerro Verde Área de manejo de hábitats y/o especies, Humedales del Santa Lucia Área Protegida con Recursos Manejados, Laureles-Canias Managed Protected Area Resource, Sierra de San Javier Parque Universitario, Horco Molle Reserva Universitaria, Aguas Chiquitas Reserva Natural, Rio Los Sosa Reserva Natural, Iberá Reserva Natural Provincial, Bahía de Samborombón Reserva Natural Integral, El Gato y Lomas Limpias Reserva de Uso Multiple, El Bagual Private Reserve, Kaa-iya del Gran Chaco, and Área de Proteção Ambiental Do Banhado Grande. Scientists think it could also live in APA do Ibirapuita, ESEC do Taim, PARES Itapeva, PARES Turvo, REBIO Lami Jose Lutzenberger, and REBIO Sao Donato. This frog lays eggs underground. When it rains, the rain helps tadpoles go to water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, human beings change the places where the frog lives to make farms. The chemicals humans use on those farms can also hurt the frogs.

The wrestler frog (Leptodactylus luctator) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Argentina. These frogs live in many places. People have seen it in grassy places, dry places, forests, outside forests, ponds, lakes, and next to rivers. It is good at living in places that human beings have changed. People sometimes see it in gardens. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. Sometimes human beings eat this frog. The frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. The foam nest stays on the top of the water. After the tadpoles hatch, they swim together in groups. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, frogs might be in danger when human beings cut down trees to get wood to build with or make farms. People also catch this frog to eat.

The San Miguel Island frog or Caribbean ditch frog (Leptodactylus insularum) is a frog. It lives in Colombia, Costa Rica, Peru, Panama, Venezuela, and Trinidad and Tobago. Scientists think it might also live in Bolivia. The adult male frog is 66–104.6 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 60.4–99.1 mm long. The skin of the frog's back has folds and dark marks on it. There is a dark line from the nose to the eye. The backs of the legs have a dark pattern on them with light spots in strange shapes. The sides of the body are light brown with dark brown spots. The belly is very light brown in color. The adult frogs use the colors on their legs to confuse bigger animals that want to eat them. These frogs live in forests near streams. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. The adult frogs eat water insects. The male frog makes a nest out of bubbles for the eggs. The female frog can lay 2000 eggs at a time. The female frog protects the eggs and tadpoles. After the eggs hatch, the female frog leads the tadpoles to deep water. If the water is about to dry up, the female frog will dig a small waterway so the tadpoles can swim to a new place. The tadpoles eat dead things that fall into the water. Sometimes people use this frog as bait when fishing. Scientists found that this frog makes peptides in its skin, for example the peptide Ocellatin-3N, that can kill germs. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. It is good at living in places that human people have changed. It can even live in the same places as the dangerous fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. B. dendrobatidis causes the disease chytridiomycosis, which kills frogs.

The Santa Fe frog (Leptodactylus laticeps) is a frog. It lives in Argentina, Bolivia, and Paraguay. These frogs live on the ground in and near forests. I can dig holes or use holes that other animals dug. Scientists saw the frog as high as 300 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places: Parque Nacional Defensores del Chaco, Parque Nacional Teniente Enciso. Scientists think it could also live in Reserva Natural Formosa, Parque Natural Provincial Fuerte Esperanza, Parque Natural Provincial Loro Hablador, and Parque Nacional Copo. Scientists are not sure how the tadpoles live. They think the tadpoles live underground. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is in a little danger of dying out. The National Red List in Argentina says it is in some danger of dying out. The National Red List in Paraguay says it is not in danger of dying out. In Paraguay and Argentina, people catch this frog to sell as a pet. People change the places where the frog lives, for example in the Chaco Seco. People change the place to make places for cows to eat grass. Fires and chemicals from farms can also hurt this frog. Big new roads like route PYIX (Transchaco) and route Bioceánica also change the frog's home.

The Guyana white-lipped frog or rugose thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus rugosus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Venezuela, and Guyana. This is a medium-sized frog. The adult male frogs have dark voice bags on their throats that they use to call. Male and female frogs have spines on their bodies, but males have more. These frogs have spots on their backs. The adult frogs are awake at night and the young frogs are awake during the day and at night. It lives in rocky, sandy places and in rainforests nearby. It sometimes lives on table-shaped land. Scientists saw the frog between 230 and 2100 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in some protected places: Kaieteur National Park and Parque Nacional Canaima. The frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. It puts the nest and eggs in shallow water. Scientists see the tadpoles swimming or moving on wet rocks. The tadpoles are brown in color with cream-white spots on their throats. Scientists from the IUCN and the Venezuela Red List say this frog is not in fclittle danger of dying out. The frogs might be in some danger when people dig good rocks out of the ground.

Miranda's white-lipped frog or Cei's white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus macrosternum) is a frog. It lives in Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Guyana, French Guiana, Suriname, Colombia, Paraguay, Peru, Venezuela, Uruguay, and Trinidad and Tobago. The adult frogs live in grassy places full of water and in forests and the edges of forests. This frog can live in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1000 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places: Chaco National Park, Mburucuyá National Park, Río Pilcomayo National Park, Parque Nacional Calilegua, San Rafael Managed Resource Reserve, Limoy Biological Reserve, Sierra de San Javier, Horco Molle Reserva Universitaria, Aguas Chiquitas Reserva Natural, Laguna Pintascayo Parque Provincial, Iberá Reserva Natural Provincial, El Bagual Private Reserve, Los Diques Reserva Provincial, Noel Kempff Mercado National Park, Kaa-iya del Gran Chaco, Otuquis National Park, Parque Nacional Da Serra Da Bodoquena, Parque Nacional Da Serra Do Divisor, Estação Ecológica Dos Caetetus, Parque Estadual Do Morro Do Diabo, and Área de Proteção Ambiental Ilhas e Várzeas do Rio Paraná. Human people used to catch this frog for fun. Now, people sometimes catch it to eat. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs in puddles and flooded places, no more than 15 cm deep. It has many young at the same time. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. The frogs might be in some danger when human beings change the places where the frogs live. Scientists from the National Red List of French Guiana say this frog is in big danger of dying out.

The Nova Teutonia white-lipped frog or gray-striped frog (Leptodactylus plaumanni) is a frog. It lives in Brazil and Argentina. Scientists think it may also live in Paraguay. The adult frogs live in grassy places and near the ends of forests. This frog can live in places where human beings have cut down the trees. The frog is good at living in places where human beings have built farms. Scientists have seen the frog between 400 and 1200 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in protected places. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. It digs a hole for the nest. The tadpoles swim in the water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, the frogs are in some danger from pine tree farms and places where cows eat grass.

The common thin-toed frog, thin-toed frog, or rana dedilarga (Leptodactylus leptodactyloides) is a frog. It lives in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador], and Peru. This frog lives in Amazonia placess. People see it in grassy places, the edges of forests, forests that were never cut down, and forests that are growing back. This frog can live in places that human beings have changed, and people see it in gardens and on farms. Scientists have seen the frog between 15 and 400 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in protected places. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. The female frog takes care of the young. She will dig a way for them to swim from one body of water to another. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, the frog is in some danger when people change the places where the frog lives.

Knudsen's frog, Knudsen's thin-toed frog, or rana dedilarga de Knudsen (Leptodactylus knudseni) is a frog. It lives in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Suriname, Venezuela, Guyana, and French Guiana, and Peru. Scientists think it could also live in Trinidad and Tobago. The adult male frog is about 94.0–170.0 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is about 102.7–154.0 mm. There is a light-colored line above the mouth. Most of these frogs have some dark triangle-shaped marks. There is a black line from the nose over each eye. There are some marks between the eyes. The belly is light in color. In Peru and Ecuador, the youngest frogs have yellow color on their heads. The iris of the eye is bronze in color. Scientists named the frog knudseni for Jens W. Knudsen, who wrote about biology. This frog lives on the ground and in holes in the ground. It lives in rainforests that were never cut down and in rainforests that are growing back, grassy places. Scientists have seen the frog between 0 and 1800 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. Scientists have only seen this frog's tadpoles in forests that have never been cut down. They saw the eggs in nests made out of bubbles. They saw the tadpoles in shallow pools of water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. It lives in a very big place and it is good at living in places that human beings have changed. People cutting down trees for wood might hurt the tadpoles.

The Campo Grande frog, Cerrado cane frog, or potter foam frog (Leptodactylus furnarius) is a frog. It lives in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. This frog lives in cerrado, Atlantic forest, and pampa places and in ponds, swamps, and grassy places. This frog is good at living in places that human beings have changed. People have seen it on Eucalyptus tree farms. Scientists have seen the frog between 200 and 1364 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in some protected places, for example APA Corumbatai, Botucatu e Tejupa Perimetro Corumbatai, APA Jalapao, PARES do Jalapao, PARES Serra do Ouro Branco, PARNA da Chapada dos Veadeiros, PARNA Grande Sertao Veredas, RPPN Estancia Santa Ines, and RPPN Olavo Egydio Setubal. The frog lays eggs underground. The tadpoles go through water to ponds. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, the frogs are in some danger when human beings change the places where the frogs live to make farms, dig metal out of the ground, or make other things that people need and use, for example dams.

The Iporanga white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus notoaktites) is a frog. It lives in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. This frog lives in places with no trees and in places at the edges of forests. Scientists have seen the frog between 0 and 900 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in some protected places. When it starts to rain, the male frog calls to the female frogs. The male frogs dig holes near shallow pools of water that dry up for part of the year. The female frog lays eggs in a nest made out of bubbles. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, the frogs are in some danger when human beings change the places where the frogs live to make towns, farms, tree farms, and places for cows to eat grass. Climate change can also hurt this frog because it can make it rain less.

Joly's frog or Joly's foam frog (Leptodactylus jolyi) is a frog. It lives in Brazil. This frog lives in cerrado, caatinga, and Atlantic forest places and in grassy places. Scientists have seen the frog between 750 and 900 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in some protected places: APA Corumbatai, Botucatu e Tejupa Perimetro Corumbatai, APA da Bacia Hidrografica do Rio do Machado, APA do Rio Sucuriu-Paraiso, APA Sul Rmbh, ESEC de Itirapina, PARES do Itacolomi, PARNA da Serra da Bodoquena, and PARNA da Serra do Cipó. The female frog lays eggs in ponds that dry up for part of the year. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, the frogs are in some danger when human beings change the places where the frogs live places for cows to eat grass and places for visitors. Climate change can also hurt this frog.

The Marambaia white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus marambaiae) is a frog. It lives in Brazil. Scientists saw this frog in one place, and island named Restinga da Marambaia. It is in the state of Rio de Janeiro. They do not think it lives anywhere else. Scientists saw the frog as high as 600 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in some protected places: Área de Proteção Ambiental de Mangaratiba and Área de Proteção Ambiental da Orla Marítima da Baía de Sepetiba. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is in a little danger of dying out. Climate change may hurt this frog.

The gray-throated thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus griseigularis) is a frog. It lives in Bolivia and Peru. This frog lives in forests that have never been cut down. Scientists have seen the frog between 100 and 1800 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in some protected places Madidi National Park and Carrasco National Park. Scientists think it could also live in Rio Abiseo National Park, Biabo Cordillera Azul Reserved Zone, Tingo Maria National Park, Yanachaga Chemillen National Park, Yanesha Communal Reserve, and Bosque de Protección San Matías San Carlos and Apurimac Reserved Zone. The female frog lays eggs in a nest made out of bubbles in water that does not move. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. It is in some danger in some parts of its home from people cutting down too many trees to make towns and farms.

Spix's white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus pascoensis) is a frog. It lives in Peru. This frog lives on the east side of the Andes mountains. The frog lives on the ground in forests. Scientists have seen the frog between 780 and 2500 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in at least one part of the Oxapampa-Asháninka-Yánesha Biosphere Reserve: Yanesha Communal Reserve. They think it might also live in El Sira Communal Reserve, Parque Nacional Yanachaga Chemillén, and Bosque de Protección San Matias San Carlos. Scientists think this frog makes a nest made out of bubbles for its eggs. Scientists from the IUCN say they do not know if the frog is in danger of dying out. Some of the places where the saw the frog are protected, so the frogs that live there are probably safe. Human beings have changed many other places nearby to make farms and places for animals to eat grass. In some places, human beings cut down many trees in the protected places even though this is against the law. People may also dig in the ground for oil soon.

The Trinidad ditch frog (Leptodactylus nesiotus) is a frog. It lives in Trinidad and Tobago, French Guiana, Guyana, and Suriname. This frog lives in grassy places not far from the ocean. People also see it in swamps and gardens. Scientists have seen the frog in a protected place in French Guiana: Amana Reserve in French Guiana. Scientists heard a male frog calling to female frogs from a hole near a fern plant in a swamp. They think the tadpoles swim in water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

Rivero's white-lipped frog (Leptodactylus riveroi) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Colombia, and Venezuela. Scientists think it may also live in Peru. This frog is awake at night. It lives on the ground. People see it in forests, next to rivers, and in swamps and gardens. Scientists have seen it between 90 and 450 meters above sea level. Scientists have seen the frog in protected places. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, human beings dig in the ground and this puts bad chemicals in the water that can hurt the frog.

The white-lipped frog or moustached frog (Leptodactylus mystacinus) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Bolivia, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina. The adult male frog is 44-65 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 54-67 mm long. The adult male has a flatter nose than the adult female. This animal has short back legs for a frog. There are white bumps on the legs. There is a light-colored stripe on the lip that people think looks like a mustache. Each frog in this species can have different colors: Some are brown with no marks, and some have darker brown stripes or spots. These frogs live in Amazonia, Chaco, Pantanal, Pampa, Atlantic Forest, Caatinga, and Cerrado places. It can live in many different kinds of places. People see it in grassy places, forests, and swamps. It is good at living in places that human beings have changed. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1800 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog in many protected places. The frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. The tadpoles can grow to be 46-48 mm long, 17-18 mm not counting the tail. The tadpoles have brown bodies and tails with both brown color and cream-white color. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. In some places, frogs might be in danger when human beings cut down many trees at the same time or make fires to make places for animals to eat grass.

The Myers' thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus myersi) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, Suriname, and French Guiana. Scientists think it could live in Guyana too. This frog lives in rocky places in rainforests. Scientists have seen it between 0 and 600 meters above sea level. There are protected places where the frog lives, for example Estação Ecológica do Grão Pará and Reserva Extrativista do Rio Cajari. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. The tadpoles swim in small rivers that form during the rainy time of year. Scientists from the IUCN and the Venezuelan Fauna Red Book say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The Gran Sabana thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus sabanensis) is a frog. It lives in Brazil and Venezuela. Scientists think it could live in Guyana too. This frog lives in grassy places, cloud forests, and evergreen forests. Scientists have seen it between 800 and 1250 meters above sea level. Most of these frogs live in a protected places: Parque Nacional Canaima. This frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs. The tadpoles swim in water. Scientists from the IUCN and the Venezuelan Fauna Red Book say this frog is not in danger of dying out.

The Pará thin-toed frog (Leptodactylus paraensis) is a frog. It lives in Brazil, in the states of Mato Grosso and Pará. The adult male frog is 99-129 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is 118-140 mm long. The skin of the frog's back is dark with marks on it. There are dark triangles on the mouth. Scientists see this frog in rainforests that have never been cut down where the branches come together like a roof. People have also seen it in forests where people cut down some trees but never cut down the whole forest. Scientists have seen these frogs in protected places, for example Tapajos National Forest. Scientists think this frog makes a nest out of bubbles for its eggs near bodies of water. After the eggs hatch, the tadpoles fall into the water. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not some danger of dying out.

The rose thigh thin-toed frog, red-thighed thin-toed frog, rana terrestre de muslos rojos, or rana dedilarga muslos roseados (Leptodactylus rhodomerus) is a frog. It lives in Ecuador and Colombia. The adult male frog is 112.2–143.8 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is about 133.5–157.8 mm long. This frog has a large body. There are three dark marks on the upper mouth that make a triangle. The skin of the frog's back is brown with a makr between the eyes. This frog is awake at night. Scientists saw the frog in rainforests and in Chaco places. Sometimes people see it in places that human beings have changed, for example places where animals eat grass. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1100 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog inside some protected places: Reserva Ecológica Cotacachi-Cayapas, Reserva Ecológica Mache Chindul, Reserva Tesoro Escondido, Estación Biológica Bilsa, Reserva Río Canandé, Reserva Awa, and Parque Nacional Los Katíos. Scientists believe it could live in many more. Human beings sometimes catch this frog to eat it. Scientists say this frog has young in streams in forests. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is not in danger of dying out. People cut down the forest where it lives to get wood to build with and make farms. Bad chemicals in rivers also hurt this frog.

The coastal dweller thin-toed frog, coastal Ecuador smoky jungle frog, or rana dedilarga de la costa (Leptodactylus peritoaktites) is a frog. It lives in Ecuador. The adult male frog is 124.0 to 146.3 mm long from nose to rear end and the adult female frog is about 115.3-133.1 mm long. This frog has a large, strong body. The skin of the frog's back is brown with two sideways stripes. The upper lip has dark marks on it, one of which can reach each eye. The eardrums and sides of the body are dark brown. The front legs have dark stripes across them. The belly is brown with cream-white spots on it. Scientists named the frog peritoaktites from the Greek words peritos for "west" and aktites for "lives next to the sea or ocean." Scientists saw the frog in rainforests in western Ecuador. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 600 meters above sea level. Scientists saw the frog inside some protected places: Bosque Protector la Perla, Mache-Chindul Ecological Reserve, and the Reserva Jama-Coaque. Human beings sometimes catch this frog to eat it. Scientists think this frog has young in streams. Scientists from the IUCN say this frog is in danger of dying out. People cut down most of the forest where it lives to get wood to build with and make farms.

The smoky jungle frog, Central American bullfrog, Savage's thin-toed frog, rana toro, or rana ternero (Leptodactylus savagei) is a frog. It lives in Colombia, Costa Rica, Honduras, Panama, and Nicaragua. Scientists believe that small insects that want to bite the frog and drink its blood find it by listening to its call. Scientists saw the frog in many places, for example forests that have never been cut down and forests that are growing back. Scientists saw the frog between 0 and 1200 meters above sea level.
